about: An introduction to quantitative social science for students with no prior statistics or coding, built around seminar practice analysing real data in R. The Department of Political Science lists it as a first-year module for BSc Philosophy, Politics and Economics (page for 2025/26). The 2026/27 catalogue page could not be accessed when this pack was checked, so the topic order here (descriptive statistics, visualisation, accessing data, probability, sampling, hypothesis testing, inference and an introduction to regression) follows the module description and should be checked against your own module page; credits, term and assessment are not given here for the same reason. Seminar syntax may differ from the R shown here, so follow your own materials.

notes.body:
Descriptive statistics summarise the data you actually have, without trying to say anything about a wider population. Two questions come first: where is the middle of the data (centre), and how much do the values vary (spread)?

Measures of centre
- Mean: add up all values and divide by n. It uses every observation, so it is pulled towards extreme values. In R: mean(x).
- Median: the middle value once the data are sorted (the average of the two middle values if n is even). It is resistant to outliers. In R: median(x).
- Mode: the most frequent value. It is the only one of the three that makes sense for nominal categories such as party. Note that R's mode() function reports an object's storage type, not the statistical mode; you tabulate with table(x) instead.

Worked example. Suppose nine local parties report annual donations (in £000): 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 46. The mean is 100/9 ≈ 11.1, the median is 7 and the mode is 5. One very large donation drags the mean well above the median. When mean > median the distribution is right-skewed (a long tail to the right). Dropping the 46 gives a mean of 6.75 and a median of 6.5, so the two nearly agree.

Measures of spread
- Range: maximum minus minimum (here 46 − 4 = 42). Very sensitive to outliers.
- Quartiles and IQR: Q1 and Q3 mark the 25th and 75th percentiles; IQR = Q3 − Q1. For the donations data, Q1 = 5, Q3 = 9 and IQR = 4 (R's default quantile() method gives these). The IQR ignores the extremes.
- Variance: the average squared distance from the mean, but using n − 1 in the denominator for a sample: s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1).
- Standard deviation: s = √s², in the same units as the data. R's var() and sd() always use n − 1, the sample formulas. For the donations data s ≈ 13.2.

Why n − 1? Deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data and so sits closer to the observations than the true population mean would. Dividing by n would therefore underestimate the population variance on average; dividing by n − 1 corrects that.

Check on a small vector: for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to 32. The population standard deviation (divide by n = 8) is exactly 2, but the sample standard deviation (divide by 7) is √(32/7) ≈ 2.14, which is what sd() returns.

Outliers and standardising
A common rule flags values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles. In the donations data the upper fence is 9 + 1.5 × 4 = 15, so 46 is flagged. A z-score re-expresses a value as the number of standard deviations from the mean: z = (x − x̄)/s. Here z for 46 ≈ (46 − 11.1)/13.2 ≈ 2.6. Z-scores let you compare values on different scales.

Skew and choice of summary
For skewed variables such as income, donations or city populations, the median and IQR describe a typical case better than the mean and standard deviation. For roughly symmetric data the mean and standard deviation are efficient and are the basis of much of inference. Report both when they differ markedly.

Level of measurement matters: the mean of a nominal variable (party coded 1, 2, 3) is meaningless, and for ordinal scales such as a five-point agreement item the median or a table of percentages is safer.

In R, summary(x) prints the minimum, quartiles, median, mean and maximum in one go; table() and prop.table() describe categorical variables.

Exam tips: always say which measure suits the shape of the data and why; remember sample variance divides by n − 1; give units; if asked to compute by hand, show the sorted data and the steps.

Graphs are the first tool of data analysis, not a decoration added at the end. A good graph reveals shape, outliers and relationships that summary numbers hide, and a bad one misleads.

Choose the chart by variable type
- One categorical variable: bar chart of counts or percentages. Bars start at zero because bar length encodes the value.
- One continuous variable: histogram (values grouped into bins, bars touching) or density plot. A histogram shows shape: symmetry, skew, several peaks. Results depend on bin width, so try more than one.
- Continuous variable across groups: side-by-side boxplots. The box spans Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median; whiskers extend to the most extreme points within 1.5 × IQR of the box and points beyond are drawn individually.
- Two continuous variables: scatterplot, optionally with a fitted line.
- Change over time: line chart, with time on the horizontal axis.

Why plot first: Anscombe's quartet
Anscombe (1973) constructed four small datasets of 11 points each. They share almost identical summary statistics: mean of x = 9, mean of y ≈ 7.5, variance of x = 11, variance of y ≈ 4.1, correlation r ≈ 0.816 and fitted regression line ŷ = 3 + 0.5x. Yet one scatterplot is a roughly linear cloud, one is a clean curve, one is a line with a single outlier, and one is a vertical stack of points with a single influential point. The lesson is that summary statistics and regression output can be identical for very different data, so always inspect a plot.

Principles of honest, readable graphics
- Label axes with variable names and units, and give the graph an informative title and source.
- Do not truncate the axis of a bar chart: starting at, say, 28 rather than 0 makes a small gap look huge. A line chart or dot plot may use a non-zero axis, but say so.
- Avoid 3D effects and decorative clutter, which distort comparisons (Tufte's data-ink principle, in The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 1983, argues for removing non-informative ink).
- Pie charts make small differences hard to judge; a sorted bar chart is usually clearer.
- Use colour with purpose, keep it readable for colour-blind viewers, and use direct labels or a clear legend.
- Show the data where possible (points or distributions, not only averages), and show uncertainty (such as confidence intervals) when you compare estimates.
- Choose the aspect ratio so slopes are not exaggerated.

Plotting in R
Base R: hist(x), boxplot(y ~ group, data = df), plot(x, y). The ggplot2 package builds graphics in layers following the "grammar of graphics" (Wilkinson, 1999; implemented by Wickham in ggplot2): you map variables to aesthetics (x, y, colour) and add geoms. For example ggplot(df, aes(x = age)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) draws a histogram, and ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a scatterplot with a linear fit. Use whichever style your seminars teach; the exam will test what a graph shows and what is wrong with it, not exact syntax.

Reading a graph critically
Ask: what are the units and scale? Is the axis truncated? How many cases are there? Are some groups too small to read? Could a third variable explain the pattern? Does a pattern across places say anything about individuals within them? A correlation in a scatterplot is not evidence of causation.

Exam tips: when asked to critique a chart, name specific problems (truncated axis, missing units, 3D, dual axes) and explain how each could mislead; when asked to choose a chart, link it to the variable type and the question.

Before any analysis you need to find data, load it into R, understand what each variable means and check it is in a usable form. Many analyses go wrong at this stage, not in the statistics.

Units, variables and levels of measurement
A dataset records variables for units of analysis (individuals, constituencies, countries, country-years). Know your unit, because conclusions apply to that level.
- Nominal: categories without order (party, region).
- Ordinal: ordered categories, gaps not necessarily equal (education level, a five-point agree/disagree scale).
- Interval: ordered with meaningful equal differences but no true zero (temperature in °C).
- Ratio: interval with a true zero, so ratios make sense (income, age, vote share).
The level of measurement limits which summaries are sensible: the mean of a nominal variable is meaningless.

Where political data come from
- Surveys: for example the British Election Study, or surveys archived at the UK Data Service. Samples with weights; responses can be affected by wording and non-response.
- Administrative and official statistics: for example the Office for National Statistics (ONS), election results from the Electoral Commission or House of Commons Library, and international bodies such as the World Bank.
- Expert-coded and constructed indices: for example V-Dem democracy indicators. These rest on measurement choices that deserve scrutiny.
Always check the codebook (variable definitions, coding of categories, missing-value codes), the date, the licence and how to cite the source.

Tidy data
Wickham (2014) defines tidy data: each variable forms a column, each observation forms a row, and each type of observational unit forms a table. A table with one row per country-year and columns country, year and gdp is tidy. A table with one row per country and a separate column for each year's GDP puts values (years) into the column names, which is a common form of untidiness. Tidy data fit R's functions and plotting tools.

Importing and inspecting in R
- Read a CSV file: df <- read.csv("file.csv") in base R, or readr::read_csv("file.csv"). Stata and SPSS files can be read with the haven package.
- Inspect immediately: head(df), str(df), dim(df), names(df) and summary(df). Check that numbers have not been read as text and that categories are coded sensibly.
- Convert categories with factor() so R treats them as groups; use levels() to see them.

Missing data
Missing values appear as NA in R and often arrive as special codes such as −99 or 9999, which you must recode to NA. Most summary functions return NA if any value is NA: mean(c(4, 8, NA, 6)) is NA, and mean(c(4, 8, NA, 6), na.rm = TRUE) is 6. Ask why data are missing; if people with certain characteristics are more likely to be missing, dropping them can bias results (complete-case analysis assumes the missingness is not systematic).

Cleaning and reproducibility
Create new variables with transformations (for example df$turnout <- df$votes / df$electorate * 100), filter cases and merge tables using a shared identifier. Keep the raw file untouched and do all changes in a script, so your analysis can be re-run from raw data to final output. Comment your code, set up a project folder, and record package versions where relevant.

Ethics and limits
Even public datasets can contain sensitive information. Use data according to its licence, do not try to identify individuals, and remember that official statistics are produced by institutions with their own definitions and sometimes revised later.

Exam tips: identify the unit of analysis and level of measurement of each variable in any scenario; explain why tidy data and a script-based workflow matter; know that NA propagates through calculations unless you handle it.

Probability is the language that links samples to populations. Inference rests on it: when we ask how likely a sample result would be under some assumption, we are using probability.

Basic rules
- A probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities of all mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes sum to 1.
- Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). If A and B cannot both happen (mutually exclusive), the last term is zero.
- Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), the probability of A given that B has happened.
- Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). If A and B are independent, P(B | A) = P(B), so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Example. Two voters are chosen independently, and each supports party X with probability 0.3. The chance that both support X is 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09. The chance that at least one does is 1 − P(neither) = 1 − 0.7² = 0.51. Adding 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6 would be wrong because it double-counts the case where both support X.

Bayes' theorem and the base-rate trap
P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B). It reverses a conditional probability. Suppose 2% of accounts in a dataset are bots, a detector flags 90% of bots, and it wrongly flags 5% of human accounts. Among all accounts, P(flagged) = 0.9 × 0.02 + 0.05 × 0.98 = 0.018 + 0.049 = 0.067. So P(bot | flagged) = 0.018 / 0.067 ≈ 0.27. Only about 27% of flagged accounts are bots, even though the detector catches 90% of bots, because bots are rare. Confusing P(flagged | bot) with P(bot | flagged) is the base-rate (or transposed-conditional) fallacy. The same confusion appears when people read a p-value as the probability that a hypothesis is true.

Random variables and expected value
A random variable takes numerical values determined by chance. Its expected value is the probability-weighted average of its values (for a fair die, 3.5). The law of large numbers says that sample means tend to settle near the expected value as the sample grows.

Binomial distribution
For n independent trials each with success probability p, the number of successes X follows a binomial distribution. For a fair coin flipped 10 times, P(X ≥ 8) = (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 = 56/1024 ≈ 0.055. In R: dbinom(k, n, p) gives P(X = k) and pbinom(k, n, p) gives P(X ≤ k), so P(X ≥ 8) is 1 − pbinom(7, 10, 0.5).

The normal distribution
The bell-shaped normal distribution is described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two (more exactly 1.96 for 95%), and about 99.7% within three. The standard normal has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and a z-score converts any normal value to it. In R: pnorm(1.96) gives P(Z ≤ 1.96) ≈ 0.975; qnorm(0.975) ≈ 1.96 reverses this; rnorm(n) simulates draws; set.seed() makes simulations reproducible.

Why the normal matters: many sample statistics, such as means, are approximately normal in large samples (the central limit theorem, covered under inference), whatever the shape of the underlying data.

Common mistakes
- Treating events as independent when they are not (sequential draws without replacement, or voters in the same household).
- The gambler's fallacy: after several heads a fair coin is not "due" tails.
- Reversing conditional probabilities.

Exam tips: write the rule you are using; define events clearly before computing; for Bayes questions, build a table or tree of 1,000 or 10,000 cases to check the arithmetic.

We rarely have data on everyone we care about. A sample is a subset of a population, and the aim of sampling is to learn about the population (a parameter, such as the proportion supporting a party) from the sample (a statistic, such as the proportion in the survey).

Key terms
- Population: the whole group of interest (for example all registered voters in Great Britain).
- Sampling frame: the list from which the sample is drawn (for example the electoral register or a list of phone numbers). A frame that misses part of the population creates coverage error.
- Probability sample: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection.
- Non-probability sample: selection chances are unknown, so formal sampling theory does not directly apply.

Probability sampling methods
- Simple random sampling: every possible sample of size n is equally likely. In R, sample(1:N, n) draws without replacement by default.
- Systematic sampling: pick every k-th unit from a list after a random start.
- Stratified sampling: divide the population into groups (strata) such as region and sample within each, which guarantees representation and can reduce variance.
- Cluster sampling: sample whole groups (constituencies, schools) and then units within them. It is cheaper but usually less precise than a simple random sample of the same size.

Non-probability methods
- Convenience samples (whoever is easy to reach).
- Quota sampling (interviewers fill quotas for age, sex, etc. but choose who to approach).
- Self-selected or opt-in samples, such as many online panels or voluntary web polls, where respondents choose to take part.
These can be useful and are widely used by pollsters with weighting and modelling, but their error cannot be summarised by the standard margin-of-error formula alone.

Sampling error versus bias
Sampling error is the random difference between a statistic and the parameter that arises because we observe only part of the population. It shrinks as n grows. Bias is a systematic tendency to miss the truth in one direction, for example because some groups are less likely to be selected or to respond. Increasing n does not remove bias. Sources include coverage error, non-response (when those who respond differ from those who do not), measurement error (question wording, social desirability) and self-selection.

Two famous illustrations. The Literary Digest poll before the 1936 US presidential election collected over two million responses, yet wrongly predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, because its sample was drawn from sources, such as telephone and car-owner lists, that over-represented wealthier voters and because response was low and unrepresentative. In Britain, the inquiry into the polls before the 2015 general election (Sturgis and colleagues, 2016) concluded that the main cause of the polling miss was unrepresentative samples, rather than late swing or misreporting of turnout.

Standard error and margin of error
For a proportion p̂ from a simple random sample of size n, the standard error is √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). The 95% margin of error is about 1.96 × SE. In the worst case (p = 0.5) with n = 1,000 it is 1.96 × √(0.25/1000) ≈ 0.031, that is about ±3.1 percentage points. Precision improves with the square root of n: quadrupling to n = 4,000 halves the margin to about ±1.5 points, whereas doubling n only reduces it by a factor of √2, to about ±2.2 points. These figures assume simple random sampling and no non-response bias; weighting and clustering typically widen real-world uncertainty.

Sampling distribution
If you drew many samples of the same size and calculated the statistic each time, the results would form its sampling distribution. Its mean is the parameter when the estimator is unbiased, and its standard deviation is the standard error. You can see this by simulation in R (replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop, 100)))). This idea underpins confidence intervals and tests.

Exam tips: distinguish random sampling error from bias and say which one a larger sample fixes; quote the √n relationship; for any survey scenario, ask who was left out of the frame and who failed to respond.

A hypothesis test asks whether sample data are surprising if a particular claim about the population is true. It does not prove a claim. It measures how compatible the data are with a stated assumption.

The logic
1. State the null hypothesis H₀ (usually 'no effect' or 'no difference', such as μ = 50) and the alternative H₁ (such as μ ≠ 50 for a two-sided test, or μ > 50 for a one-sided test).
2. Choose a significance level α in advance, conventionally 0.05.
3. Compute a test statistic that measures how far the sample result is from what H₀ predicts, in standard-error units.
4. Find the p-value: the probability, if H₀ (and the other assumptions of the test) were true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
5. If p < α, reject H₀; otherwise fail to reject it. Failing to reject is not the same as showing H₀ is true.

Worked example. Suppose a sample of n = 25 gives mean 53.2 and standard deviation 8, and we test H₀: μ = 50 against a two-sided alternative. The standard error is 8/√25 = 1.6, so t = (53.2 − 50)/1.6 = 2.0 with 24 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is about 0.057. Since 0.057 > 0.05 we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level. (Using the normal distribution instead would give p ≈ 0.046, which crosses the threshold, so with a small sample using the t distribution matters.) In R: t.test(x, mu = 50).

A discrete example. If a coin is fair, the probability of 8 or more heads in 10 flips is 56/1024 ≈ 0.055, a one-sided p-value. For a two-sided test of 'the coin is fair' we count equally extreme results in both tails, giving about 0.109.

What a p-value is not
- It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and 1 − p is not the probability that H₁ is true. A p-value is calculated assuming H₀ is true.
- It is not the probability that the result was 'due to chance'.
- It does not measure the size or importance of an effect. With a large sample, tiny effects can have very small p-values.
- A p-value above 0.05 does not show 'no effect'; the study may have lacked power.

Errors and power
- Type I error: rejecting H₀ when it is true. The significance level α is the maximum probability of this error that the test allows when H₀ holds, so with α = 0.05 about 5% of tests of true nulls would reject.
- Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it is false. Its probability is usually written β.
- Power = 1 − β: the probability of rejecting a false null. It rises with sample size, with larger true effects and with a larger α.

Statistical versus substantive significance
Report the estimate and its uncertainty as well as p. A 0.2-point difference in an attitude scale may be statistically significant in a big survey but politically trivial.

Multiple testing and p-hacking
If you run 20 independent tests of true null hypotheses at α = 0.05, you expect about one false positive. Trying many outcomes, subsets or specifications and reporting only the 'significant' ones inflates false positives. Pre-specify hypotheses and report all tests carried out.

Confidence intervals and tests
A two-sided test at level α = 0.05 rejects H₀: μ = μ₀ exactly when μ₀ lies outside the 95% confidence interval for μ. In the example, the 95% interval for the mean (about 49.9 to 56.5) contains 50, consistent with not rejecting.

Exam tips: write H₀ and H₁ in terms of population parameters; state the decision in context and in words ('we do not reject at the 5% level'); never say the p-value is the probability that H₀ is true.

Inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about a population while quantifying uncertainty. The two main tools are confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, both built on sampling distributions.

Standard error and the central limit theorem
The standard error (SE) of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. For a sample mean it is σ/√n, usually estimated by s/√n. For a proportion it is √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).

The central limit theorem says that, for reasonably large samples, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, centred on the population mean, whatever the shape of the population distribution (provided it has finite variance). This is why normal-based inference works for means and proportions in large samples. How large is 'large' depends on how skewed the data are.

Confidence intervals
A 95% confidence interval for a mean is estimate ± critical value × SE. When σ is estimated from the data, use the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails than the normal when n is small.

Worked example. n = 25, mean 53.2, s = 8. SE = 8/5 = 1.6. The t critical value with 24 degrees of freedom is about 2.064, so the interval is 53.2 ± 2.064 × 1.6, about 49.9 to 56.5. Using 1.96 instead (the normal value) would give a slightly too narrow 50.1 to 56.3, and using s = 8 instead of the SE would produce 36.7 to 69.7, which is far too wide because it describes the spread of individuals, not of the mean.

For a proportion. A poll of 1,000 finds 52% support. SE = √(0.52 × 0.48/1000) ≈ 0.0158, so the 95% interval is 0.52 ± 1.96 × 0.0158, about 48.9% to 55.1%. The interval includes 50%, so the poll alone does not show a majority.

How to interpret a confidence interval
The 95% describes the procedure: if we repeated the sampling and built an interval this way each time, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true parameter. Once an interval has been calculated, it either contains the parameter or does not; it is not correct to say there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains it, or that 95% of individual observations fall inside it. Higher confidence gives wider intervals, and larger n gives narrower ones.

Comparing two groups
Suppose group 1 (n = 40) has mean 62 and standard deviation 10, and group 2 (n = 50) has mean 57 and standard deviation 12. The difference is 5. With unequal variances (the Welch approach, which is R's default in t.test()), SE = √(10²/40 + 12²/50) = √5.38 ≈ 2.32, t ≈ 2.16, with about 87.8 degrees of freedom, and the two-sided p-value is about 0.034. The 95% interval for the difference is about 0.4 to 9.6. Because zero lies outside the interval, the test rejects 'no difference' at the 5% level. In R: t.test(y ~ group, data = df).

Other common tests
- Test or interval for a proportion: prop.test(x, n).
- Association between two categorical variables: chisq.test(table(a, b)) compares observed counts with those expected if the variables were independent.
- Correlation: cor(x, y) gives Pearson's r; cor.test(x, y) tests whether the population correlation is zero.

Assumptions
Standard methods assume random (or as-if random) sampling and independent observations. Clustered or panel data violate independence and require adjusted methods. A confidence interval does not correct for bias, as it only reflects random sampling error.

Exam tips: state the interval formula and the critical value you use; interpret the interval in context without saying 'there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval'; link intervals and tests (does the interval contain the null value?).

Linear regression models how the average of an outcome variable y changes with a predictor x. It is the workhorse of quantitative social science.

The model and ordinary least squares
The simple linear regression model is y = α + βx + ε. The fitted line is ŷ = a + bx, where the intercept a and slope b are chosen by ordinary least squares (OLS) to minimise the sum of squared residuals, the vertical gaps between observed and fitted values. The formulas are b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)² and a = ȳ − b x̄. The fitted line always passes through (x̄, ȳ).

Worked example. Take five observations: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). Then x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 6 and Σ(x − x̄)² = 10, so b = 0.6 and a = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2. The fitted line is ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x. The residuals are −0.8, 0.6, 1.0, −0.6, −0.2 (they sum to zero), and the sum of squared residuals is 2.4.

Interpreting coefficients
- Slope: a one-unit increase in x is associated with a b-unit change in the predicted value of y, on average. Here, each extra unit of x goes with 0.6 more units of y. Say 'associated with', not 'causes', unless the design justifies a causal reading.
- Intercept: the predicted y when x = 0. It may not be meaningful if x = 0 lies outside the data.
- With a binary (dummy) predictor, the slope is the difference in mean y between the two groups.
- Prediction: when x = 4, ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6 × 4 = 4.6. The observed value at x = 4 is 4, so the residual is −0.6. Avoid extrapolating beyond the range of observed x.

Fit
R² is the proportion of the sample variation in y accounted for by the fitted line. Here R² = 0.6, equal to r² with r ≈ 0.775 in simple regression. A high R² does not mean x causes y, and a low R² does not mean the slope is unimportant. The residual standard error, √(SSR/(n − 2)) = √(2.4/3) ≈ 0.894, is the typical size of a residual in the units of y.

Inference about the slope
The standard error of the slope is s/√Σ(x − x̄)², here 0.894/√10 ≈ 0.283. The t statistic is b/SE = 0.6/0.283 ≈ 2.12 with n − 2 = 3 degrees of freedom, giving a two-sided p-value of about 0.124. The 95% interval is 0.6 ± 3.182 × 0.283, about −0.30 to 1.50. With only five points the data cannot rule out a zero slope. In R: m <- lm(y ~ x, data = df); summary(m) reports estimates, standard errors, t values, p-values, the residual standard error and R². confint(m) gives intervals, and predict() gives fitted values.

The R summary for this example would show: intercept 2.2 (SE 0.938, t = 2.35, p ≈ 0.10), x 0.6 (SE 0.283, t = 2.12, p ≈ 0.12), residual standard error 0.894 on 3 degrees of freedom, multiple R² 0.6.

OLS assumptions (for the standard properties)
- Linearity: the mean of y is a linear function of x (in the parameters).
- Exogeneity: the error term has mean zero given x, with x unrelated to omitted factors. This is what makes the estimate unbiased; it fails with omitted variable bias or reverse causation.
- Constant variance (homoskedasticity) and uncorrelated errors, needed for the usual standard errors to be correct.
- No perfect multicollinearity among predictors (multiple regression).
- Normally distributed errors are not required for unbiasedness; they matter mainly for exact small-sample t tests.
Check residual plots for curvature, non-constant variance and influential points.

Multiple regression and causation
Adding further predictors lets you compare cases that are equal on those variables ('holding constant'), reducing confounding from measured variables. It cannot remove confounding from unmeasured variables, so regression coefficients are descriptive unless the research design (for example randomisation) supports a causal interpretation. Correlation does not imply causation: a third variable may drive both x and y.

Exam tips: interpret slopes in words and units with 'on average'; give the prediction by substituting; note R² is a description of fit, not proof of causation; state at least one assumption and what happens if it fails.

cards.b: The sum of the values divided by n. It uses all observations, so it is pulled towards extreme values and is not resistant to outliers.
The middle value of the sorted data (average of the two middle values if n is even). Resistant to outliers, so often preferred for skewed variables like income.
The statistical mode is the most frequent value; find it with table(x). R's mode() function does not do this: it reports an object's storage type.
s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1). Dividing by n − 1 rather than n corrects the underestimate that comes from measuring deviations around the sample mean.
Interquartile range: Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of values. It ignores the extremes, so it is resistant to outliers.
A common outlier flag: values below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. It is the convention behind the whiskers of a standard boxplot.
In a right-skewed distribution the long tail pulls the mean above the median, so mean > median is a sign of right skew.
z = (x − x̄)/s: how many standard deviations a value lies above (+) or below (−) the mean. Lets you compare values measured on different scales.
A histogram bins a continuous variable (touching bars, order fixed, shape depends on bin width). A bar chart shows counts or values for categories, with gaps between bars.
Box = Q1 to Q3, line = median. Whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR of the box; points beyond are plotted individually as potential outliers.
Four 11-point datasets with near-identical means, variances, correlation (r ≈ 0.816) and regression line, but very different scatterplots. Always plot your data.
Starting a bar chart's value axis above zero exaggerates differences, because bar length is meant to encode the value from zero.

cards.f: Best chart for two continuous variables
cards.b: A scatterplot, optionally with a fitted line. It shows form (linear or curved), strength, direction and outliers.
Tufte (1983): maximise the share of ink that conveys data and remove chart junk and decoration that adds nothing, such as 3D effects.
Plots are built in layers: map variables to aesthetics with aes(), then add geoms such as geom_histogram() or geom_point().
Too narrow gives a noisy picture, too wide hides structure. Try several bin widths before concluding the distribution is, say, single-peaked.
Nominal categories have no order (party). Ordinal categories are ordered but the gaps between them are not necessarily equal (a five-point agreement scale).
Both have equal intervals. Only ratio scales have a true zero, so ratios make sense (income, age); temperature in °C is interval.
Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit is a table. One row per country-year is tidy.
Documentation listing each variable's meaning, coding of categories and missing-value codes. Read it before analysing any dataset.
R's missing-value marker. mean(c(4, 8, NA, 6)) returns NA; add na.rm = TRUE to compute the mean of the non-missing values.
Datasets often use values like −99 or 9999 for missing. If you do not recode them to NA, they will be treated as real numbers and distort results.
Use head(), str(), dim(), names() and summary() to check variable types, categories and obvious errors before any analysis.
A script records every cleaning and analysis step, keeps the raw data untouched and makes the work reproducible and checkable.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Often the easiest route to 'at least one' questions: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Only when A and B are mutually exclusive does it reduce to P(A) + P(B).
A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A): learning B tells you nothing about A.
P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B): the probability of A within the cases where B has occurred.
P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B). It reverses conditional probabilities and shows the importance of the base rate P(A).
Treating P(B | A) as if it were P(A | B), ignoring how rare A is. A highly sensitive test can still produce mostly false alarms when the condition is rare.
The number of successes in n independent trials with the same success probability p. In R, dbinom() gives exact probabilities and pbinom() cumulative ones.
About 68% of values within 1 sd of the mean, about 95% within 2 sd (precisely 1.96), about 99.7% within 3 sd.
A parameter describes the population (usually unknown). A statistic describes the sample and is used to estimate the parameter.
The list from which a sample is drawn. If it omits part of the population, the result is coverage error.
Every possible sample of size n has the same chance of being drawn, so each unit has an equal chance of selection.
Stratified: divide into groups and sample within every group, which guarantees representation. Cluster: sample whole groups, then units within them, which is cheaper but usually less precise.
Sampling error is random and shrinks as n grows. Bias is systematic (for example non-response or self-selection) and does not go away with a bigger sample.

cards.f: Margin of error for a poll
cards.b: About 1.96 × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) for a simple random sample. With n = 1,000 and p̂ = 0.5 it is about ±3.1 percentage points.

cards.f: Effect of sample size on precision
cards.b: The standard error falls with √n. To halve the margin of error you need four times the sample size.
More than two million responses but a wrong prediction (Landon over Roosevelt), because of an unrepresentative sampling frame and low, unrepresentative response. Big n does not fix bias.
The default claim tested, usually 'no effect' or 'no difference' (for example μ = 50). The test asks whether the data are surprising if H₀ is true.
The probability, assuming H₀ (and the test's other assumptions) is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
Not the probability that H₀ is true, not the probability the result was 'due to chance', and not a measure of the size or importance of an effect.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). The significance level α caps its probability when H₀ is true.
Type II: failing to reject a false null (probability β). Power = 1 − β, the chance of detecting a real effect; it rises with sample size and effect size.
It means the data are not sufficiently inconsistent with H₀. It does not show that H₀ is true: the test may have low power.
With large samples tiny effects can be statistically significant. Always report effect size and uncertainty and judge practical importance separately.
Running many tests at α = 0.05 produces false positives by chance (about 1 in 20 true nulls). Reporting only significant results inflates error rates (p-hacking).
s/√n: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean. It describes uncertainty about the mean, not spread of individuals.
For large samples the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal, centred on the population mean, whatever the shape of the data (finite variance assumed).
x̄ ± t* × s/√n, with t* from the t distribution with n − 1 df. For large n, t* is close to 1.96.
Because s replaces σ, which adds uncertainty. The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, with the difference shrinking as df rises.
If we repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter. It is not a 95% probability for one calculated interval.
A two-sided 5% test rejects H₀: parameter = value exactly when the value lies outside the 95% confidence interval.
A two-sample t-test that does not assume equal variances. It is R's default in t.test(), with degrees of freedom calculated from the group variances.
Ordinary least squares chooses the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals (vertical distances from points to the line).
b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)², and the intercept a = ȳ − b x̄, so the line passes through the point (x̄, ȳ).
A one-unit increase in x is associated with a b-unit change in the predicted y, on average. It is a causal effect only if the design supports that reading.
The proportion of sample variation in y accounted for by the model. In simple regression it equals the square of the correlation r.
t = b/SE(b) with n − 2 degrees of freedom in simple regression, testing H₀: the population slope is zero.
If a variable that affects y is correlated with x and left out, the estimated slope picks up part of its effect, so exogeneity fails and the estimate is biased.

cards.f: Is normal error needed for unbiased OLS?
cards.b: No. Unbiasedness needs linearity and exogeneity (error mean zero given x). Normal errors matter mainly for exact small-sample t and F tests.
Predicting for x values outside the observed range relies on the linear pattern continuing, which the data cannot support. Avoid or flag it.

questions.q: In R, sd(c(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9)) returns approximately which value?
questions.why: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to 32. sd() uses the sample formula, so it computes √(32/7) ≈ 2.14. A result of 2.00 divides by n = 8 and is the population standard deviation, which R does not report by default. The figure 4.57 is the sample variance (32/7), not its square root. The figure 4.00 is the population variance (32/8).

questions.q: Nine party donations (£000) are 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 46. Which statement about them is correct?
options: The mean (about 11.1) is greater than the median (7), because the single large value pulls the mean up much more than the median
The median is 5, because that is the value that occurs most often
The mean is the better summary of a typical party, because it uses every value and so is unaffected by 46
The median is 25, halfway between the smallest and largest values
questions.why: The sum is 100, so the mean is 11.1, while the middle (fifth) of the sorted values is 7. Saying the median is 5 confuses it with the mode. Using every value is exactly why the mean is not resistant: 46 pulls it upwards. Halfway between the extremes (4 and 46) is the midrange, not the median.

questions.q: The values 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 46 are annual donations (£000) to nine local parties. Calculate the median and the IQR (using quartiles 5 and 9 as given by R's default method) and say whether 46 is an outlier under the 1.5 × IQR rule.
markScheme: Median = 7 (fifth of nine sorted values)
Upper fence = 9 + 1.5 × 4 = 15
46 > 15, so it is flagged as an outlier
questions.modelAnswer: Sorted, the fifth value is 7, so the median is 7. With Q1 = 5 and Q3 = 9 the IQR is 4. The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 9 + 6 = 15, and 46 is far above it, so it is an outlier by this rule. (The lower fence, 5 − 6 = −1, flags nothing.) The rule is a convention for flagging cases to inspect, not proof that the value is an error.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of Anscombe's quartet (1973)?
options: The correlation coefficient detects curved relationships as well as straight-line ones
Datasets with near-identical summary statistics and regression lines can look completely different when plotted, so you should always graph the data
Regression results are unreliable whenever there are only 11 observations
Outliers should always be deleted before computing a correlation
questions.why: Anscombe's four datasets share means, variances, r ≈ 0.816 and the same fitted line, but their scatterplots differ sharply. The sample size of 11 is not the point of the demonstration. Automatically deleting outliers is not what he recommends, since one dataset has an outlier and another a single influential point that need inspecting. Pearson's r measures linear association only, and one of the four datasets is a clear curve with the same r.

questions.q: A bar chart compares mean incomes of two groups, but its vertical axis starts at £28,000 instead of £0, so one bar looks several times taller. What is wrong?
options: The truncated axis exaggerates the difference, because bar length is supposed to be proportional to the value measured from zero
The chart would be fixed by making the bars three-dimensional, which makes heights easier to compare
Means cannot be compared graphically without a histogram
Bar charts can only show counts of cases, never means
questions.why: Bar length encodes magnitude from a zero baseline, so starting at £28,000 makes the visual ratio far larger than the real ratio. Bar charts can show any summary value, including means, so the idea that they only show counts is wrong. Three-dimensional bars add distortion rather than removing it. A histogram shows the distribution of one variable and is not required to compare two means.

questions.q: A scatterplot suggests a strong positive linear relationship, and the correlation is 0.8. Give three things you should check on the graph before relying on that figure.
markScheme: Outliers or influential points driving the correlation
Whether the pattern is actually linear (curvature)
Whether subgroups (a third variable) create or hide the pattern
Scale, units and number of cases; correlation is not causation
questions.modelAnswer: First, look for outliers or a single influential point: one extreme case can create or inflate a correlation (Anscombe's quartet). Second, check the relationship is roughly linear, because Pearson's r only measures linear association and can be low or high for curved patterns. Third, ask whether distinct subgroups mix together, so a pooled pattern differs from the pattern within groups. Also check the units, the range and the sample size. Even a clean linear pattern shows association, not that x causes y.

questions.q: Under Wickham's (2014) definition of tidy data, which layout is best for analysing GDP across countries and years?
options: A separate table for each year, each with a different layout
One row per country, with a separate column for each year's GDP value
One row per country-year, with separate columns for country, year and GDP
A single text column holding entries like "UK, 2019, 2.8" for each observation
questions.why: Tidy data put each variable in its own column and each observation in its own row, so country-year rows with country, year and GDP columns qualify. Putting a column per year places the values of the variable year in the column names, a standard form of untidiness. Packing several variables into one text column breaks the one-variable-per-column rule. Splitting the data into separate tables per year leaves the same variable spread across tables, and it makes plotting over time harder.

questions.q: In R, x <- c(4, 8, NA, 6). What does mean(x) return?
options: An error message because the vector contains text
NA
questions.why: Without na.rm = TRUE, any NA makes the mean NA, because R does not assume what the missing value is. The value 6 is what you get by adding na.rm = TRUE, which drops the NA before averaging. The value 4.5 would come from treating the NA as zero ((4 + 8 + 0 + 6)/4), which R does not do. NA is a recognised missing marker, not text, so no error occurs.

questions.q: You download a country-level dataset from an international organisation. List four checks you would make before using it in an analysis.
markScheme: Read the codebook: definitions, units, coding of categories
Inspect structure with head/str/summary; check variable types
Identify and recode special missing codes to NA; consider why data are missing
Check unit of analysis, time period, source, licence and citation
questions.modelAnswer: I would first read the codebook so I know what each variable measures, in what units and with which category codes. After importing I would inspect it with head(), str() and summary() to check that numeric variables are numeric and that values are plausible. I would look for special codes such as −99 and recode them to NA, and think about whether missingness is systematic, since dropping those cases could bias results. Finally I would confirm the unit of analysis and time coverage, check whether the data are tidy, and note the source, licence and how to cite it.

questions.q: 2% of accounts in a dataset are bots. A detector flags 90% of bots and wrongly flags 5% of human accounts. An account is flagged. What is the probability, to the nearest percentage point, that it is a bot?
questions.why: P(bot and flagged) = 0.9 × 0.02 = 0.018 and P(flagged) = 0.018 + 0.05 × 0.98 = 0.067, so P(bot | flagged) ≈ 0.27. The figure 90% is the detector's sensitivity, P(flagged | bot), which is the transposed conditional. The figure 2% is the base rate before the flag is observed. The figure 95% is the share of humans correctly left unflagged, which says nothing about how many flagged accounts are bots.

questions.q: Two voters are chosen independently. Each supports party X with probability 0.3. What is the probability that at least one supports party X?
questions.why: Use the complement: 1 − P(neither supports X) = 1 − 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.51. The value 0.60 adds 0.3 and 0.3 and so double-counts the case where both support X. The value 0.09 is the probability that both support X (0.3 × 0.3). The value 0.49 is the probability that neither supports X, which is the complement of what is asked.

questions.q: A fair coin is flipped 10 times. (a) State the distribution of the number of heads. (b) Calculate the probability of 8 or more heads, and give the R command. (c) What is the probability of 8 or more heads or 8 or more tails?
markScheme: Binomial with n = 10, p = 0.5
By symmetry, 8+ tails has the same probability and the events cannot both occur, so 2 × 56/1024 ≈ 0.109
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The number of heads is binomial with n = 10 trials and p = 0.5. (b) The ways to get 8, 9 and 10 heads are C(10,8) = 45, C(10,9) = 10 and C(10,10) = 1, out of 2¹⁰ = 1024 equally likely sequences, so P(X ≥ 8) = 56/1024 ≈ 0.055. In R: 1 - pbinom(7, 10, 0.5). (c) 8 or more tails is the same event as 2 or fewer heads, and has the same probability by symmetry. The two events cannot both happen in 10 flips, so the addition rule gives 56/1024 + 56/1024 = 112/1024 ≈ 0.109.

questions.q: A pollster has a margin of error of about ±3.1 points from a simple random sample of 1,000. Assuming the same proportion, what sample size gives a margin of about ±1.5 points?
options: About 2,000
About 16,000
About 500
About 4,000
questions.why: The margin of error is proportional to 1/√n, so halving it requires four times the sample: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 (giving about ±1.5 points). Doubling to 2,000 assumes error falls in proportion to n, but it only falls to about ±2.2. A sample of 16,000 would quarter the margin, a confusion between halving and quartering. A sample of 500 reverses the relationship, since a smaller sample widens the margin to about ±4.4.

questions.q: A student society runs an opt-in online survey about voting and gets 3,000 responses, mostly from very politically engaged members. Which statement is correct?
options: Bias disappears once a sample is larger than about 1,000
It is a probability sample because every respondent chose to take part
Because n = 3,000, the margin-of-error formula guarantees the result is within about ±1.8 points of the population value
Self-selection can bias the estimates, and collecting more responses of the same kind does not remove that bias
questions.why: Respondents differ systematically from non-respondents, and extra responses from the same kind of people only make the biased estimate more precise. The ±1.8 figure is 1.96 × √(0.25/3000) and applies only to simple random samples, not to self-selected ones. There is no sample size beyond which bias vanishes; the Literary Digest had millions of responses and was still wrong. A probability sample requires known, non-zero selection chances set by the researcher, which self-selection does not provide.

questions.q: Explain the difference between sampling error and bias in a survey, and say which of them increasing the sample size can reduce. Give one example of each.
markScheme: Sampling error = random variation between samples; shrinks as n rises (SE ∝ 1/√n)
Bias = systematic departure from the truth
Increasing n reduces sampling error but not bias
Example of sampling error, e.g. different random samples give slightly different poll shares
Example of bias, e.g. non-response by a particular group, coverage error, self-selection
questions.modelAnswer: Sampling error is the random difference between a sample statistic and the population value because only part of the population is observed. Different random samples give slightly different results, and the standard error shrinks in proportion to 1/√n, so a larger sample reduces it. Bias is a systematic tendency to err in one direction. For example, if younger people are less likely to respond to a phone survey, the estimate will understate their views however many people are interviewed. A bigger sample therefore reduces sampling error but not bias; fixing bias needs a better frame, better response and weighting, or a different design.

questions.q: A test of a treatment effect gives p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
If there were truly no effect (and the test's assumptions held), results at least this extreme would occur with probability 0.03
The effect is large and politically important
questions.why: A p-value is computed on the assumption that H₀ is true, and reports how unusual the data would be under it. It is not the probability that the null itself is true, because the p-value is calculated assuming it is, and the 97% figure makes the same mistake in reverse. A small p-value says nothing directly about effect size, since very small effects can give small p-values in large samples.

questions.q: A researcher tests many true null hypotheses, each at α = 0.05. In the long run, about what proportion of these tests will (wrongly) reject?
options: About 5%
About 95%
None, because a true null can never be rejected
More as the sample size increases, because larger samples find more false positives
questions.why: The significance level fixes the long-run Type I error rate when the null is true, here about 5%. The figure 95% is the confidence level, the share of non-rejections when the null is true, not the rejection rate. Rejection of a true null does occur by chance, so the claim that it cannot happen is wrong. For a correctly specified test, the false-positive rate stays at α however large the sample; what grows with n is the ability to detect real (including trivial) effects.

questions.q: A sample of 25 people has mean 53.2 and standard deviation 8. Test H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ ≠ 50 at the 5% level. Show the standard error, the test statistic, and your conclusion.
markScheme: Two-sided p ≈ 0.057 (critical t ≈ 2.064)
p > 0.05 so do not reject H₀ at the 5% level
Interpretation: data are not sufficiently inconsistent with μ = 50; this does not prove μ = 50
questions.modelAnswer: The standard error is 8/√25 = 1.6, so t = (53.2 − 50)/1.6 = 2.0 with n − 1 = 24 degrees of freedom. The two-sided critical value at the 5% level is about 2.064 and the p-value is about 0.057. Because t is below the critical value (p above 0.05), we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level. This does not show the mean is exactly 50: it says a sample mean this far from 50 is not unusual enough, under H₀, to rule 50 out at this level. The 95% interval, about 49.9 to 56.5, contains 50, which agrees.

questions.q: A sample of 25 has mean 53.2 and standard deviation 8. Which is the correct 95% confidence interval for the population mean (t critical value with 24 df ≈ 2.064)?
questions.why: SE = 8/√25 = 1.6 and the margin is 2.064 × 1.6 ≈ 3.3, giving 49.9 to 56.5. The interval 50.1 to 56.3 uses 1.96 (the normal value), which ignores the extra uncertainty from estimating the standard deviation. The interval 36.7 to 69.7 uses the standard deviation of 8 where the standard error belongs, so it describes the spread of individuals. The interval 52.5 to 53.9 divides the standard deviation by n (25) rather than √n (5), producing a far too small SE of 0.32.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is calculated as 49.9 to 56.5. Which statement is the best interpretation?
options: 95% of individual observations lie between 49.9 and 56.5
If the sampling and interval construction were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true population mean
There is a 95% probability that a new sample's mean will fall between 49.9 and 56.5
There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies between 49.9 and 56.5
questions.why: The confidence level refers to the long-run success rate of the method. The probability statement about this one interval is wrong in the frequentist framework because the true mean is fixed and the calculated interval either contains it or does not. The interval is built from the standard error of the mean, so it is much narrower than the range containing most individual observations. A future sample mean is not guaranteed to land inside, since it varies around the true mean, not around this particular estimate.

questions.q: A poll of 1,000 randomly selected adults finds 52% support for a policy. Calculate an approximate 95% confidence interval and say what it tells you about whether a majority of the population supports the policy.
markScheme: Margin ≈ 1.96 × 0.0158 ≈ 3.1 points
Interval ≈ 48.9% to 55.1%
Interval includes 50%: cannot conclude majority support
Caveat: assumes random sampling; bias is not captured
questions.modelAnswer: The standard error is √(0.52 × 0.48/1000) ≈ 0.0158 (1.6 percentage points). The 95% margin is 1.96 × 0.0158 ≈ 0.031, so the interval is about 48.9% to 55.1%. Because 50% lies inside the interval, the poll is compatible with the policy having less than, equal to, or more than majority support, so we cannot conclude a majority supports it. This relies on a simple random sample; non-response or coverage problems would not be reflected in the interval.

questions.q: A regression of y on x for five observations gives ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x. What is the predicted value of y when x = 4?
questions.why: Substitute: 2.2 + 0.6 × 4 = 4.6. The value 2.4 is 0.6 × 4 with the intercept forgotten. The value 4.0 is the observed y at x = 4, which differs from the prediction by the residual of −0.6. The value 5.2 is the prediction for x = 5, an off-by-one reading of the wrong row.

questions.q: In a simple regression, R² = 0.60. What does this mean?
options: 60% of the observations lie exactly on the fitted line
The fitted line accounts for 60% of the sample variation in y
x causes 60% of the changes in y
The correlation between x and y is 0.60
questions.why: R² is the share of the variation in y that the fitted line accounts for in the sample, and it is purely descriptive of fit. It says nothing about causal shares. In simple regression R² equals r², so r would be about 0.775, not 0.60. A high R² does not require points to lie on the line; in OLS with scatter, few or none may lie exactly on it.

questions.q: A hypothetical regression of voter turnout (%) on the percentage of residents with a degree across constituencies gives a slope of 0.4 with a standard error of 0.1 (n = 102). (a) Interpret the slope. (b) Is it statistically significant at the 5% level? (c) Can we conclude that raising graduate numbers would raise turnout? Explain.
markScheme: Interpretation: each extra percentage point of graduates is associated with 0.4 points higher turnout on average
t = 0.4/0.1 = 4, with 100 df; p far below 0.05 so significant
Association, not causation: confounding by omitted variables (for example age, income)
Ecological point: the data are about constituencies, not individuals
Possible reverse causation or selection
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Across constituencies, each additional percentage point of residents with a degree is associated with turnout that is on average 0.4 percentage points higher. (b) t = 0.4/0.1 = 4 with n − 2 = 100 degrees of freedom, which gives a p-value far below 0.05, so the slope differs significantly from zero at the 5% level. (c) No. The result describes association. Constituencies with more graduates may differ in age, income, urbanisation or other factors that also affect turnout, so omitted variables could produce the pattern, and the data cannot show that changing graduate numbers would change turnout. Also, the unit is the constituency, so the finding does not tell us how individual graduates behave.

questions.q: A researcher studying five towns records x (units of local-party campaign activity) and y (turnout index) and gets the pairs (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). (a) Calculate the OLS regression line. (b) Compute the residuals and R². (c) Calculate the standard error of the slope, the t statistic and a 95% confidence interval (t critical value for 3 df is 3.182). (d) Interpret your findings and discuss whether they show that campaign activity affects turnout.
markScheme: Means x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4; Sxy = 6, Sxx = 10; slope 0.6 and intercept 2.2
Conclusion: not significant at 5%; sample is tiny; interval includes zero and substantively large effects
Causation: confounders, reverse causation, only five cases; association not effect
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 4. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = (−2)(−2) + (−1)(0) + 0(1) + (1)(0) + (2)(1) = 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6, and Σ(x − x̄)² = 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10. So the slope is b = 6/10 = 0.6 and the intercept is a = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2, giving ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x.

(b) The fitted values are 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6 and 5.2, so the residuals y − ŷ are −0.8, 0.6, 1.0, −0.6 and −0.2, which sum to zero. The sum of squared residuals is 0.64 + 0.36 + 1.00 + 0.36 + 0.04 = 2.4. The total sum of squares Σ(y − ȳ)² is 4 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 6, so R² = 1 − 2.4/6 = 0.6, which equals r² for r ≈ 0.775.

(c) The residual standard error is √(2.4/(5 − 2)) = √0.8 ≈ 0.894. The standard error of the slope is 0.894/√10 ≈ 0.283. Then t = 0.6/0.283 ≈ 2.12 with 3 degrees of freedom, a two-sided p-value of about 0.124. The 95% confidence interval is 0.6 ± 3.182 × 0.283 ≈ 0.6 ± 0.90, i.e. about −0.30 to 1.50.

(d) The estimated association is positive: each extra unit of campaign activity goes with 0.6 more units of turnout index on average. But with only five towns the estimate is imprecise: the slope is not significant at the 5% level, and the interval includes zero as well as sizeable positive effects, so the data are compatible with no relationship and with a substantial one. Fitting a line to five points is also sensitive to single cases, so plotting is essential. Even a significant slope would not show causation: towns with more campaign activity might differ in competitiveness, resources or demography, and turnout could itself attract campaigning (reverse causation). A causal claim would need a design that handles these issues, such as randomisation or credible controls with more cases.

questions.q: A think tank publishes the result of an opt-in online poll of 3,000 people and reports that 56% support a policy, claiming 'a clear majority, with a margin of error of ±1.8 points'. (a) Explain how the margin of error is calculated and what assumptions it makes. (b) Evaluate whether the claim is justified. (c) Describe how a better design could address the problems. (d) Explain what a 95% confidence interval would and would not tell us even for a well-designed random sample.
markScheme: Margin of error = 1.96 × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n); with p = 0.5, n = 3000 it is about 1.8 points
Assumes simple random sampling, full response, accurate answers: not satisfied by an opt-in sample
Self-selection and coverage bias; larger n does not remove bias; weighting limited
The headline interval would be about 54.2% to 57.8% if random, but unreliable here
Better design: probability sample from a good frame, follow-up non-response, weighting, report uncertainty honestly
CI interpretation: long-run procedure, not probability for one interval; no protection against bias or wording effects
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For a simple random sample, the 95% margin of error for a proportion is about 1.96 × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). Using the worst case p̂ = 0.5 and n = 3,000, this is 1.96 × √(0.25/3000) ≈ 0.018, that is ±1.8 percentage points. The calculation assumes that respondents were chosen at random from the population, that nearly everyone chosen responded, and that responses are accurate. Under those assumptions, the only error is random sampling error.

(b) The claim is not justified. In an opt-in poll the sample is self-selected, so selection chances are unknown and respondents are likely to differ from the population, for example by being more online, more politically engaged or more interested in the think tank's topic. This is bias, not random error, so the ±1.8 figure does not describe the real uncertainty. Adding more respondents of the same kind makes the estimate more precise around a biased value, as the Literary Digest's two million responses showed. Weighting to match known demographics can reduce some bias but cannot guarantee that people with the same demographics hold the same views. With a genuine random sample the interval would be about 54.2% to 57.8%, which would exclude 50%, but that conclusion cannot be drawn from this design.

(c) A better design draws a probability sample from a good frame (such as an address list), follows up non-respondents, weights to known population margins, tests question wording and reports a margin of error that reflects the design effect from weighting. Researchers can also compare their sample against external benchmarks, such as official statistics.

(d) Even for a random sample, a 95% confidence interval describes a procedure: across repeated samples, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true proportion. It does not give a 95% probability for this one interval, and it does not capture bias from non-response, coverage or question wording. It also says nothing about how intensely people hold views or whether the opinion would change if more information were given.
